e23.original_source_text:
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode

workflow = StateGraph(MessagesState)

# Define the nodes to cycle between
workflow.add_node(generate_query_or_respond)
workflow.add_node("retrieve", ToolNode([retriever_tool]))
workflow.add_node(rewrite_question)
workflow.add_node(generate_answer)

workflow.add_edge(START, "generate_query_or_respond")

# Route based on whether the model requested tool calls.
def route_on_tool_calls(state: MessagesState):
    last_message = state["messages"][-1]
    if getattr(last_message, "tool_calls", None):
        return "tools"
    return END

# Decide whether to retrieve
workflow.add_conditional_edges(
    "generate_query_or_respond",
    # Assess LLM decision (call `retriever_tool` tool or respond to the user)
    route_on_tool_calls,
    {
        # Translate the condition outputs to nodes in our graph
        "tools": "retrieve",
        END: END,
    },
)

# Edges taken after the `action` node is called.
workflow.add_conditional_edges(
    "retrieve",
    # Assess agent decision
    grade_documents,
)
workflow.add_edge("generate_answer", END)
workflow.add_edge("rewrite_question", "generate_query_or_respond")

graph = workflow.compile()

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
SECTION: I. INTRODUCTION
LABEL: Fig. 1
OBJECT IDENTITY: Fig. 1. Technology tree of RAG research.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Fig. 1. Technology tree of RAG research. The stages of involving RAG mainly include pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference. With the emergence of LLMs, research on RAG initially focused on leveraging the powerful in-context learning abilities of LLMs, primarily concentrating on the inference stage. Subsequent research has delved deeper, gradually integrating more with the fine-tuning of LLMs. Researchers have also been exploring ways to enhance language models in the pre-training stage through retrieval-augmented techniques.

Visual structure: the figure is a stylized tree drawn on a light background. A single root block at the bottom is labelled 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation'. From that root, three trunks grow upward, each a separate augmentation stage and each drawn in its own color, matching the legend box at the lower right titled 'Augmentation Stage': Fine-tuning (teal/green), Pre-training (orange), Inference (dark blue). Branch titles appear at the top of each trunk: 'Fine-tuning' (left), 'Pre-training' (middle), 'Inference' (right). A vertical time axis runs down the left edge with, from bottom to top, the markers 2020, GPT-3, ChatGPT, 2023, GPT-4, 2024; the LLM-release markers (GPT-3, ChatGPT, GPT-4) are drawn in pink pills while the year markers (2020, 2023, 2024) are grey, and horizontal dashed guide lines extend from 2020, 2023 and 2024 across the tree. Each leaf is a green rounded label carrying one method name; leaf vertical position encodes its position on the time axis.

Leaves on the Fine-tuning trunk (bottom to top, both sides): RAG, Atlas, Zemi, PROMPTAGATOR, RAG-e2e, R-GQA, UPRISE, Self-Mem, FLARE, AAR, RRR, SUGRE, SANTA, Retrieve-and-Sample, RAG_Robust, MK-ToD, LM-Indexer, RA-DIT, Dual-Feedback-ToD, Self-RAG, RAST, EAR, CoN, BEQ, CT-RAG, UniMS-RAG.

Leaves on the Pre-training trunk (bottom to top): TIGER, Retro++, RAVEN, CoG, InstructRetro.

Leaves on the Inference trunk (bottom to top, both sides): RECITE, GenRead, DSP, ICRALM, RePLUG, LLM-IE, Filter-Reranker, COQ, SCM4LLMs, ITER-RETGEN, PKG, LLM-R, PGRA, KGP, IRCOT, KnowledGPT, ITRG, SKR, Recomp, KALMV, QLM-Doc-ranking, Token-Elimination, FABULA, PRCA, 1-PAGER, ToC, ARM-RAG, FILCO, PaperQA, CREA-ICL, IAG, HyKGE, DRAGON-AI, CRAG, G-Retriever, RAPTOR, RADA, BGM.

The figure carries no numeric axis other than the year markers, and no quantitative values.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The source caption identifies the figure as a technology tree organised by the three RAG augmentation stages, matching the three trunks drawn in the image.
- The source caption explains the pre-training trunk, which in the image carries only five leaves.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- Several leaf labels in the image differ from the names used in TABLE I of the same paper: the image shows 'BEQ' where TABLE I lists 'BEQUE [9]', 'SUGRE' where TABLE I lists 'SURGE [77]', and 'RAG_Robust' where TABLE I lists 'RAG-Robust [48]'. The image labels are reported as drawn; they are not corrected here.
- Leaf labels 'KGP', 'LLM-IE', 'SCM4LLMs' and 'DRAGON-AI' appear in the image but have no corresponding row in TABLE I of the supplied source Markdown.
- The caption rendered inside the PNG says 'in context learning'; the source Markdown caption says 'in-context learning'. Both are recorded rather than silently normalised.

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
SECTION: A. Naive RAG
LABEL: Fig. 2
OBJECT IDENTITY: Fig. 2. A representative instance of the RAG process applied to question answering.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Fig. 2. A representative instance of the RAG process applied to question answering. It mainly consists of 3 steps. 1) Indexing. Documents are split into chunks, encoded into vectors, and stored in a vector database. 2) Retrieval. Retrieve the Top k chunks most relevant to the question based on semantic similarity. 3) Generation. Input the original question and the retrieved chunks together into LLM to generate the final answer.

Visual structure: a left-to-right then right-to-left flow diagram with four shaded group panels, each carrying a title: 'Input' (yellow, top centre), 'Indexing' (purple, top right), 'Retrieval' (pink, right), 'Generation' (blue, bottom left/centre).

Nodes and direction. A 'User' box at the left sends an arrow into the Input panel, which holds a 'Query' node whose dashed box contains the worked example question: 'How do you evaluate the fact that OpenAI's CEO, Sam Altman, went through a sudden dismissal by the board in just three days, and then was rehired by the company, resembling a real-life version of "Game of Thrones" in terms of power dynamics?'. From the Query the flow splits: one arrow goes right into the Indexing panel and one arrow goes down into the 'LLM' node in the Generation panel. Inside the Indexing panel a stack icon labelled 'Documents' feeds an arrow into a stack of horizontal bars labelled 'Chunks Vectors'; an 'embeddings' node sits below the Indexing panel and feeds down into the Retrieval panel. In the Retrieval panel a 'Relevant Documents' node points down to a dashed box listing three retrieved chunks: 'Chunk 1: "Sam Altman Returns to OpenAI as CEO, Silicon Valley Drama Resembles the 'Zhen Huan' Comedy"', 'Chunk 2: "The Drama Concludes? Sam Altman to Return as CEO of OpenAI, Board to Undergo Restructuring"', 'Chunk 3: "The Personnel Turmoil at OpenAI Comes to an End: Who Won and Who Lost?"'. An arrow runs leftwards from that chunk box into a 'Combine Context and Prompts' node, which feeds the prompt box in the Generation panel. The prompt box shows 'Question:' followed by an abbreviated form of the query, then 'Please answer the above questions based on the following information:' and the placeholders 'Chunk 1:', 'Chunk 2:', 'Chunk 3:'. The prompt box connects to the 'LLM' node, drawn with a snowflake icon indicating a frozen model.

Output branch: the LLM produces two contrasting answers inside the 'Answer' group. The upper one is labelled 'without RAG' with a sad-face icon and a grey cross mark, text: '...I am unable to provide comments on future events. Currently, I do not have any information regarding the dismissal and rehiring of OpenAI's CEO ...'. The lower one is labelled 'with RAG' with a smiling-face icon and an orange check mark, text: '......This suggests significant internal disagreements within OpenAI regarding the company's future direction and strategic decisions. All of these twists and turns reflect power struggles and corporate governance issues within OpenAI...'. An arrow labelled 'Output' runs from the Answer group back up to the 'User' node, closing the loop.

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
SECTION: B. Advanced RAG
LABEL: Fig. 3
OBJECT IDENTITY: Fig. 3. Comparison between the three paradigms of RAG.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Fig. 3. Comparison between the three paradigms of RAG. (Left) Naive RAG mainly consists of three parts: indexing, retrieval and generation. (Middle) Advanced RAG proposes multiple optimization strategies around pre-retrieval and post-retrieval, with a process similar to the Naive RAG, still following a chain-like structure. (Right) Modular RAG inherits and develops from the previous paradigm, showcasing greater flexibility overall. This is evident in the introduction of multiple specific functional modules and the replacement of existing modules. The overall process is not limited to sequential retrieval and generation; it includes methods such as iterative and adaptive retrieval.

Visual structure: three side-by-side panels, each with a bold blue title at the bottom: 'Naive RAG' (left), 'Advanced RAG' (middle), 'Modular RAG' (right).

Left panel, Naive RAG. Top row holds two boxes: 'User / Query' (person and query icons) and 'Documents' (link, file and stack icons). A thick arrow runs from Documents down to 'Indexing'. Arrows from 'User / Query' and from 'Indexing' both run down into 'Retrieval'. From 'Retrieval' an arrow runs down into a box containing 'Prompt' with a grey arrow to 'Frozen LLM' (snowflake icon), and from there down to 'Output'. The chain is therefore User/Query and Documents -> Indexing -> Retrieval -> Prompt -> Frozen LLM -> Output.

Middle panel, Advanced RAG. Same top row ('User / Query' and 'Documents'). The query side now passes through an orange box titled 'Pre-Retrieval' with three bulleted items: 'Query Routing', 'Query Rewriting', 'Query Expansion'. The documents side still passes through 'Indexing'. Both feed 'Retrieval'. Below 'Retrieval' an orange box titled 'Post-Retrieval' holds three icon-labelled operations: 'Rerank', 'Summary', 'Fusion'. Its output goes to 'Prompt' -> 'Frozen LLM' (snowflake) -> 'Output'. The chain remains linear.

Right panel, Modular RAG. It is split into two labelled sub-areas. The upper sub-area is titled 'Modules' and shows ten module boxes arranged around a central 'RAG' label, linked by dashed lines: 'Search' (top), 'Routing' (upper left), 'Predict' (upper right), 'Retrieve' (inner top), 'Rewrite' (inner left), 'Rerank' (inner right), 'Read' (inner bottom), 'Demonstrate' (lower left), 'Fusion' (lower right), 'Memory' (bottom). The four inner boxes Retrieve, Rewrite, Rerank and Read are outlined in orange; the outer six are outlined in blue. The lower sub-area is titled 'Patterns' and shows four vertical pipelines, each with its own label underneath: 'Naive RAG' = Retrieve -> Read; 'Advanced RAG' = Rewrite -> Retrieve -> Rerank -> Read; 'DSP [Khattab et al.,2022]' = Demonstrate -> Search -> Predict; 'ITER-RETGEN [Shao et al., 2023]' = Retrieve -> Read -> Retrieve -> Read with a return arrow from the final Read back up to the first Retrieve, drawing the iterative loop.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The source caption fixes the left-to-right ordering of the three panels as Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG.
- The source caption motivates the loop-back arrow drawn in the ITER-RETGEN pattern of the Modular RAG panel.

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
SECTION: A. Retrieval Source
LABEL: Fig. 4
OBJECT IDENTITY: Fig. 4. RAG compared with other model optimization methods in the aspects of “External Knowledge Required” and “Model Adaption Required”.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Fig. 4. RAG compared with other model optimization methods in the aspects of 'External Knowledge Required' and 'Model Adaption Required'. Prompt Engineering requires low modifications to the model and external knowledge, focusing on harnessing the capabilities of LLMs themselves. Fine-tuning, on the other hand, involves further training the model. In the early stages of RAG (Naive RAG), there is a low demand for model modifications. As research progresses, Modular RAG has become more integrated with fine-tuning techniques.

Visual structure: a qualitative two-axis schematic, not a data plot. The vertical axis is labelled 'External Knowledge Required' and is annotated only with 'Low' at the bottom and 'High' near the top. The horizontal axis is labelled 'Model Adaptation Required' and is annotated only with 'Low' at the left and 'High' at the right. There are no tick values, no units and no numeric scale.

Nodes and direction: a vertical ladder of six boxes rises along the left, each linked to the next by a dashed upward arrow, giving the progression Standard Prompt -> Few-shot Prompt -> 'XoT Prompt e.g. CoT, ToT' -> 'Naive RAG / Add relevant contextual paragraphs' -> 'Advanced RAG / Index/pre-retrieval/post-retrieval optimization' -> 'Modular RAG / Organic combination of multiple modules'. From Modular RAG a dashed arrow runs right and then curves down into the region labelled 'All of the above'.

Groups: three shaded blobs plus one named region are placed in the plane. An orange blob in the middle is labelled 'RAG'; a blue blob to its lower right is labelled 'Fine-tuning'; a pale region in the upper right is labelled 'All of the above'; the text 'Prompt Engineering' sits in the lower-left area of the plane. Thin dashed leader lines connect Naive RAG, Advanced RAG and Modular RAG to the 'RAG' blob, and connect Standard Prompt, Few-shot Prompt and XoT Prompt to the 'Prompt Engineering' area. Three callout boxes on the right are joined by dashed leaders to the 'All of the above' region: 'Retriever Fine-tuning', 'Collaborative Fine-tuning' and 'Generator Fine-tuning'. A dashed curve sweeps across the plane separating the lower/left prompting area from the upper/right RAG and fine-tuning areas.

Supported reading: position on the plane is the only quantity encoded — prompting methods sit at low external-knowledge and low model-adaptation, RAG variants rise on the external-knowledge axis, Fine-tuning sits further along the model-adaptation axis, and the 'All of the above' region is at high values on both axes.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The source caption names the two axes of the schematic.
- The source caption supports the dashed arrow drawn from the Modular RAG box into the 'All of the above' region.

- Conflict between figure and source caption: the horizontal axis inside the PNG is labelled 'Model Adaptation Required', while the caption in the source Markdown writes 'Model Adaption Required'. Both spellings are recorded; neither is silently corrected.
- The figure is a conceptual placement diagram: relative positions carry meaning but no numeric values can be read off it.

As research progresses, Modular RAG has become more integrated with fine-tuning techniques.

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
SECTION: A. Iterative Retrieval
LABEL: Fig. 5
OBJECT IDENTITY: Fig. 5. In addition to the most common once retrieval, RAG also includes three types of retrieval augmentation processes.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Fig. 5. In addition to the most common once retrieval, RAG also includes three types of retrieval augmentation processes. (left) Iterative retrieval involves alternating between retrieval and generation, allowing for richer and more targeted context from the knowledge base at each step. (Middle) Recursive retrieval involves gradually refining the user query and breaking down the problem into sub-problems, then continuously solving complex problems through retrieval and generation. (Right) Adaptive retrieval focuses on enabling the RAG system to autonomously determine whether external knowledge retrieval is necessary and when to stop retrieval and generation, often utilizing LLM-generated special tokens for control.

Visual structure: three flowchart panels side by side. Each panel has a title bar and a one-line subtitle: 'ITERATIVE — Provide more context information' (left, blue), 'RECURSIVE — Break down complex problems step by step' (middle, purple), 'ADAPTIVE — Flexible and active control of retrieval and generation' (right, orange). In all three panels 'Query' and 'Response' are green rounded boxes, processing steps are grey rounded boxes, and decision points are orange diamonds labelled 'Judge'. Solid blue arrows carry the forward flow; dashed blue arrows carry the feedback/loop edges.

Left panel (ITERATIVE): Query -> Retrieve -> Generate -> Judge. From Judge a dashed arrow loops back up to Retrieve, annotated 'Iterate N Times'. The forward exit from Judge goes down to Response and is annotated with the stopping condition 'Max Times / Threshold'.

Middle panel (RECURSIVE): Query -> Retrieve -> Generate -> Judge. From Judge a dashed arrow goes right into a box 'Query Transformation / Decomposition', and from that box a dashed arrow returns up and left into Retrieve, forming the recursion. The forward exit from Judge goes down to Response and is annotated 'Max Depth (Tree) / Threshold'.

Right panel (ADAPTIVE): Query -> Judge (first decision, annotated on its right with 'Retrieve On Demand'). This first Judge has two branches: a dashed branch going left to a standalone 'Generate' box, which then feeds a dashed arrow down and right into Response, i.e. answering without retrieval; and a solid branch going down to Retrieve -> Generate -> a second Judge. From the second Judge a dashed arrow goes right into a box 'Query Transformation / Decomposition', which loops back by a dashed arrow into Retrieve. The forward exit from the second Judge goes down to Response and is annotated 'Generate Special Token / Threshold'.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The source caption establishes that the three panels are three retrieval augmentation processes distinct from single-pass retrieval.
- The source caption explains the 'Generate Special Token / Threshold' stopping annotation drawn in the ADAPTIVE panel.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- The ADAPTIVE subtitle is printed with a double space, as 'Flexible and  active control of retrieval and generation'; preserved as drawn in visible_facts.

ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
TABLE IV — SUMMARY OF EVALUATION FRAMEWORKS (Gao et al., 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey').

Four columns: Evaluation Framework | Evaluation Targets | Evaluation Aspects | Quantitative Metrics. Each framework occupies one block; within a block the Evaluation Aspects and Quantitative Metrics are paired line by line, and the Evaluation Targets cell applies to the whole block.

RGB (dagger): Evaluation Targets = Retrieval Quality, Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric pairs: Noise Robustness -> Accuracy; Negative Rejection -> EM; Information Integration -> Accuracy; Counterfactual Robustness -> Accuracy.

RECALL (dagger): Evaluation Targets = Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric: Counterfactual Robustness -> R-Rate (Reappearance Rate).

RAGAS (double dagger): Evaluation Targets = Retrieval Quality, Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric pairs: Context Relevance -> *; Faithfulness -> *; Answer Relevance -> Cosine Similarity.

ARES (double dagger): Evaluation Targets = Retrieval Quality, Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric pairs: Context Relevance -> Accuracy; Faithfulness -> Accuracy; Answer Relevance -> Accuracy.

TruLens (double dagger): Evaluation Targets = Retrieval Quality, Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric pairs: Context Relevance -> *; Faithfulness -> *; Answer Relevance -> *.

CRUD (dagger): Evaluation Targets = Retrieval Quality, Generation Quality. Aspect -> Metric pairs: Creative Generation -> BLEU; Knowledge-intensive QA -> ROUGE-L; Error Correction -> BertScore; Summarization -> RAGQuestEval.

Footnote printed below the table: 'dagger represents a benchmark, and double dagger represents a tool. * denotes customized quantitative metrics, which deviate from traditional metrics. Readers are encouraged to consult pertinent literature for the specific quantification formulas associated with these metrics, as required.' Accordingly RGB, RECALL and CRUD are benchmarks and RAGAS, ARES and TruLens are tools.

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
SECTION: 1 Introduction
LABEL: Figure 1
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 1: Overview of our approach.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 1: Overview of our approach. We combine a pre-trained retriever (Query Encoder + Document Index) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (Generator) and fine-tune end-to-end. For query x, we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents z_i. For final prediction y, we treat z as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents.

Visual structure: a left-to-right architecture diagram with two large outlined blocks in the middle. The left block is green and titled 'Retriever p_eta (Non-Parametric)'; it contains a tall bar labelled 'Query Encoder' with the inner node 'q', an arrow to the embedded query 'q(x)', an arrow to the label 'MIPS', and a group titled 'Document Index' holding a stack of five document cards labelled z_1 through z_4 (the frontmost card is shaded purple and the remaining cards are white, with small green bars beside them denoting retrieval scores d(z)). The right block is blue and titled 'Generator p_theta (Parametric)'; it contains a tall bar with the inner node 'p_theta' and, at its output, the label 'Marginalize'.

Inputs on the far left: three example query boxes, each with an '(x)' marker and a task caption underneath. Top: 'Define "middle ear"' captioned 'Question Answering: Question Query'. Middle: 'Barack Obama was born in Hawaii.' captioned 'Fact Verification: Fact Query'. Bottom: 'The Divine Comedy' captioned 'Jeopardy Question Generation: Answer Query'. A line runs from the input side along the bottom of the retriever block back into the Document Index area.

Outputs on the far right: three example generation boxes, each with a '(y)' marker and a task caption underneath. Top: 'The middle ear includes the tympanic cavity and the three ossicles.' captioned 'Question Answering: Answer Generation'. Middle: 'supports' captioned 'Fact Verification: Label Generation'. Bottom: 'This 14th century work is divided into 3 sections: "Inferno", "Purgatorio" & "Paradiso"' captioned 'Question Generation'.

Across the top a long dashed arrow points right-to-left, labelled 'End-to-End Backprop through q and p_theta', indicating that gradients flow back through both the query encoder and the generator. Two solid arrows run from the retrieved documents into the generator block, and one solid arrow runs from the generator to the output examples.

For query _x_ , we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents _zi_ . For final prediction _y_ , we treat _z_ as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents.

Inside the retriever, the sub-labels 'Query Encoder', 'q', 'q(x)', 'MIPS', 'Document Index' and 'd(z)' appear, with document cards labelled z_1, z_2, z_3 and z_4.
The generator block contains the node 'p_theta' and the output label 'Marginalize'.
A dashed arrow across the top, pointing from the generator side back to the input side, is labelled 'End-to-End Backprop through q and p_theta'.

Three example inputs are shown, each marked (x): 'Define "middle ear"' (Question Answering: Question Query), 'Barack Obama was born in Hawaii.' (Fact Verification: Fact Query), 'The Divine Comedy' (Jeopardy Question Generation: Answer Query).

Three example outputs are shown, each marked (y): 'The middle ear includes the tympanic cavity and the three ossicles.' (Question Answering: Answer Generation), 'supports' (Fact Verification: Label Generation), 'This 14th century work is divided into 3 sections: "Inferno", "Purgatorio" & "Paradiso"' (Question Generation).

TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
SECTION: 4 Results > 4.4 Fact Verification
LABEL: Figure 2
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 2: RAG-Token document posterior for each generated token
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 2: RAG-Token document posterior p(z_i | x, y_i, y_-i) for each generated token for input 'Hemingway' for Jeopardy generation with 5 retrieved documents. The posterior for document 1 is high when generating 'A Farewell to Arms' and for document 2 when generating 'The Sun Also Rises'.

Visual structure: the figure has two parts. On the left is a text panel quoting two of the retrieved documents. 'Document 1: his works are considered classics of American literature ... His wartime experiences formed the basis for his novel "A Farewell to Arms" (1929) ...'. 'Document 2: ... artists of the 1920s "Lost Generation" expatriate community. His debut novel, "The Sun Also Rises", was published in 1926.' The novel titles are set in bold in both documents.

On the right is a single-panel heatmap. The vertical axis lists five rows labelled top to bottom 'Doc 1', 'Doc 2', 'Doc 3', 'Doc 4', 'Doc 5'. The horizontal axis lists the generated tokens in order, written diagonally: BOS, ", The, Sun, Also, R, ises, ", is, a, novel, by, this, author, of, ", A, Fare, well, to, Arms, ". Each cell is shaded on a white-to-dark-blue color scale representing the posterior probability of that document for that token; no numeric scale, colour bar or units are printed.

Supported trends: the darkest cell in the Doc 1 row falls on the token 'A' at the start of 'A Farewell to Arms', with the neighbouring 'Fare' cell also noticeably dark; the darkest cell in the Doc 2 row falls on the token 'Sun' within 'The Sun Also Rises'. Rows Doc 3, Doc 4 and Doc 5 stay uniformly pale across all tokens, i.e. no strongly peaked posterior. These are relative shading comparisons only; no precise probabilities can be read from the image.

- RAG-S: 'It's the state where you'll find Mount Rainier National Park'

text:
TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
SECTION: 4 Results > 4.5 Additional Results
LABEL: Figure 3
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 3: Left: NQ performance as more documents are retrieved. Center: Retrieval recall performance in NQ. Right: MS-MARCO Bleu-1 and Rouge-L as more documents are retrieved.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 3: Left: NQ performance as more documents are retrieved. Center: Retrieval recall performance in NQ. Right: MS-MARCO Bleu-1 and Rouge-L as more documents are retrieved.

Visual structure: three line-plot panels side by side. All three share the same x-axis label, 'K Retrieved Docs', running from about 0 to 50 with ticks at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50.

Left panel. Y-axis label 'NQ Exact Match', ticks from 39 to 44. Legend with two series: 'RAG-Tok' (solid orange) and 'RAG-Seq' (dashed green). Both curves rise steeply for very small K. RAG-Tok peaks at roughly K just under 10 near 43.6 and then declines slowly and flattens near 43.0 by K = 50. RAG-Seq rises above RAG-Tok at around K = 5, continues rising more gradually, and plateaus near 44.1 from about K = 20 onward. The two curves cross once, at small K.

Center panel. Y-axis label 'NQ Answer Recall @ K', ticks from 40 to about 82. Legend with four series: 'RAG-Tok' (solid orange), 'RAG-Seq' (dashed green), 'Fixed DPR' (dash-dotted blue) and 'BM25' (dotted pink). All four curves increase monotonically with K. RAG-Tok and RAG-Seq lie almost on top of each other and highest, reaching roughly 82 at K = 50. Fixed DPR runs slightly below them, reaching roughly 81 at K = 50. BM25 is far below the other three across the whole range, starting lowest and reaching roughly 65 at K = 50.

Right panel. Y-axis label 'Bleu-1 / Rouge-L score', ticks from 48 to 56 and above. Legend with four series: 'RAG-Tok R-L' (solid orange), 'RAG-Tok B-1' (dash-dotted orange), 'RAG-Seq R-L' (dashed green) and 'RAG-Seq B-1' (dashed green). The two Rouge-L curves sit in the upper part of the panel and are essentially flat after a small initial rise, with RAG-Seq R-L slightly above RAG-Tok R-L, both a little above 56. The two Bleu-1 curves sit in the lower part of the panel, decline slightly from their K-small values and then stay flat, with RAG-Tok B-1 around 49 and RAG-Seq B-1 around 47.5 at large K.

All stated values are approximate readings off the axes; the panels print no data labels.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The source caption fixes the subject of each of the three panels in left-to-right order.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- Numeric readings given in the description are approximations taken from axis ticks; the figure prints no exact values.
- In the right panel's legend, the 'RAG-Seq R-L' and 'RAG-Seq B-1' entries are both drawn as green dashed lines at this resolution, so the two are distinguished by their vertical position (Rouge-L above, Bleu-1 below) rather than by line style.

parameters. The best performing "closed-book" (parametric only) open-domain QA model is T5-11B with 11 Billion trainable parameters. The T5 model with the closest number of parameters to our models is T5-large (770M parameters), which achieves a score of 28.9 EM on Natural Questions [52], substantially below the 44.5 that RAG-Sequence achieves, indicating that hybrid parametric/nonparametric models require far fewer trainable parameters for strong open-domain QA performance. The non-parametric memory index does not consist of trainable parameters, but does consists of 21M 728 dimensional vectors, consisting of 15.3B values. These can be easily be stored at 8-bit floating point precision to manage memory and disk footprints.

TITLE: Rerankers and Two-Stage Retrieval
SECTION: Recall vs. Context Windows
OBJECT IDENTITY: When storing information in the middle of a context window, an LLM's ability to recall that information becomes worse than had it not been provided in the first place [2].
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Hand-drawn style line chart on a white background, with black arrow-headed axes and faint horizontal gridlines. The image has no printed title.

The vertical axis is labelled "Accuracy (%)" and carries tick labels 55, 60, 65, 70 and 75. The horizontal axis is labelled "Position of Doc in context" (written on two lines below the axis) and carries the tick labels "1st", "5th", "10th", "15th" and "20th".

Two series are annotated directly on the plot instead of in a legend box. A thick solid blue polyline is labelled, in blue handwriting at the upper right, "gpt-3.5-turbo (with context)", with the word "with" highlighted in yellow. A flat horizontal dashed grey-blue line is labelled below that, in grey-blue handwriting, "gpt-3.5-turbo (no context)", with the word "no" highlighted in yellow.

Reading the blue polyline against the gridlines, all values approximate: it starts highest at the "1st" position at roughly 75%, falls steeply to about 57% at "5th", declines further to its minimum of roughly 54% at about the "10th" position, recovers slightly to about 55-56% at "15th", then rises more steeply to about 63% at "20th". The dashed no-context baseline is flat at about 56%. Consequently the blue curve is drawn above the dashed baseline at the "1st" position and at the "20th" position, and below the baseline across the middle of the range, roughly from just after "5th" until just before "15th".

The chart shows no numeric data labels, no error bars, no shaded confidence band and no reference citation inside the image. The overall shape is a U with a higher left shoulder than right shoulder.

- The caption line printed directly beneath the image anchor in the source; it states the middle-of-context degradation the plotted curve illustrates and cites reference [2].
- Exact image anchor for this visual.
- The sentence immediately preceding the anchor, establishing that the chart is about LLM recall rather than retrieval recall.
- Following prose defining LLM recall and attributing the underlying research to reference [2].

- The pre-existing description contained only the surrounding prose and caption; it made no assertion at all about the plotted axes, series or curve shape. The visual content has been added.
- All numeric readings are approximate values read off the drawn gridlines. The chart prints no data labels, so no exact figure should be attributed to it.
- The citation marker [2] appears in the source caption but not inside the image; the image itself is uncited and names no dataset or benchmark.
- The caption speaks of "ability to recall" while the y-axis is labelled "Accuracy (%)". The axis label has been reported as drawn rather than restated as recall.

ORIGINAL CAPTION/SOURCE:
When storing information in the middle of a context window, an LLM's ability to recall that information becomes worse than had it not been provided in the first place [2].

LLM recall refers to the ability of an LLM to find information from the text placed within its context window. Research shows that LLM recall degrades as we put more tokens in the context window [2]. LLMs are also less likely to follow instructions as we stuff the context window — so context stuffing is a bad idea.

We can increase the number of documents returned by our vector DB to increase retrieval recall, but we cannot pass these to our LLM without damaging LLM recall.

The solution to this issue is to maximize retrieval recall by retrieving plenty of documents and then maximize LLM recall by _minimizing_ the number of documents that make it to the LLM. To do that, we reorder retrieved documents and keep just the most relevant for our LLM — to do that, we use _reranking_.

TITLE: Rerankers and Two-Stage Retrieval
SECTION: Power of Rerankers
OBJECT IDENTITY: A two-stage retrieval system. The vector DB step will typically include a bi-encoder or sparse embedding model.
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Hand-drawn diagram of a two-stage retrieval system on a white background, flowing from the top of the image downward and then to the right. The image carries no printed title.

At the top, the handwritten label "All documents" sits above a long horizontal bar that is subdivided into many thin vertical cells, standing for the whole corpus. Two straight lines run inward from the two ends of that bar and funnel down into a hand-drawn cylinder labelled "Vector DB" on two lines.

On the left of the figure, the label "Query:" sits above a scribbled squiggle that ends in a question mark, standing in for the user's query text. A horizontal arrow runs from the squiggle rightwards into the cylinder and carries the handwritten label "top_k = 25" above it.

Below the cylinder a second funnel narrows down into a tall vertical stack of thin horizontal cells, representing the retrieved records. Three of those cells are filled yellow: one near the top of the stack, one roughly two thirds of the way down, and one at the bottom. Dashed brackets on the left of the stack connect those three yellow cells to the handwritten note "These are most relevant records".

Two straight lines leave the top and bottom of that stack and converge to the left and bottom vertices of a cyan-filled diamond labelled "Reranker". Two further straight lines leave the diamond and fan out to the right toward a third vertical stack at the far right edge; the handwritten label "top_n = 3" is written above those lines.

The right-hand stack is drawn in two parts. The upper part has a solid outline and contains three yellow-filled cells stacked together. Below it, separated by the stack boundary, a taller block is drawn entirely with dashed outlines and contains several empty cells plus one yellow-filled cell. The solid-outlined yellow group at the top corresponds to the three records kept by the reranker and the dashed block below to the records that are dropped.

- The exact number of cells in the corpus bar and in the retrieved stack is not countable reliably from the drawing; only the three highlighted cells and the labelled values top_k = 25 and top_n = 3 are stated.

ORIGINAL CAPTION/SOURCE:
A two-stage retrieval system. The vector DB step will typically include a bi-encoder or sparse embedding model.

Search engineers have used rerankers in two-stage retrieval systems for _a long time_. In these two-stage systems, a first-stage model (an embedding model/retriever) retrieves a set of relevant documents from a larger dataset. Then, a second-stage model (the reranker) is used to rerank those documents retrieved by the first-stage model.

We use two stages because retrieving a small set of documents from a large dataset is much faster than reranking a large set of documents — we'll discuss why this is the case soon — but TL;DR, rerankers are slow, and retrievers are _fast_.

We use two stages because retrieving a small set of documents from a large dataset is much faster than reranking a large set of documents — we'll discuss why this is the case soon — but TL;DR, rerankers are slow, and retrievers are _fast_.

ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 2: Core Components of RAG. A single left-to-right pipeline with one return edge, drawn as a closed loop that starts and ends at the user.

Nodes and direction: a stick-figure icon labelled "User" sits at the left. A solid arrow runs from the User to a blue box labelled "Retrieval"; a solid arrow runs from "Retrieval" to an orange box labelled "Augmentation"; a solid arrow runs from "Augmentation" to a pink box labelled "Generation". From the right-hand side of "Generation" a long curved arrow sweeps down and back to the left, is annotated with the word "Response" along its path, and terminates with an arrowhead at the "User" icon.

There are no branches, conditions or loops other than this single feedback edge, and no sub-groups. The three coloured boxes are the only processing stages shown, so the figure asserts exactly the three-stage decomposition Retrieval -> Augmentation -> Generation, with the generated answer returned to the user who issued the request.

The figure carries no labels for data stores, models, or tools; those details appear only in the body text of Section 2.2, which defines Retrieval as querying external data sources such as knowledge bases, APIs or vector databases, Augmentation as extracting and summarising the retrieved data to match the query context, and Generation as combining the retrieved information with the LLM's pre-trained knowledge.

Table 1: Comparative Analysis of RAG Paradigms, from the survey "Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG" (Singh et al.), page 8, Section 2.4.1. The title is printed above the table in the image. Three columns — "Paradigm", "Key Features", "Strengths" — and five data rows, one per RAG paradigm. Feature and strength cells are bulleted lists. Full contents:

Row 1 — Paradigm: Naive RAG. Key Features: Keyword-based retrieval (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25). Strengths: Simple and easy to implement; Suitable for fact-based queries.

Row 2 — Paradigm: Advanced RAG. Key Features: Dense retrieval models (e.g., DPR); Neural ranking and re-ranking; Multi-hop retrieval. Strengths: High precision retrieval; Improved contextual relevance.

Row 3 — Paradigm: Modular RAG. Key Features: Hybrid retrieval (sparse and dense); Tool and API integration; Composable, domain-specific pipelines. Strengths: High flexibility and customization; Suitable for diverse applications; Scalable.

Row 4 — Paradigm: Graph RAG. Key Features: Integration of graph-based structures; Multi-hop reasoning; Contextual enrichment via nodes. Strengths: Relational reasoning capabilities; Mitigates hallucinations; Ideal for structured data tasks.

Row 5 — Paradigm: Agentic RAG. Key Features: Autonomous agents; Dynamic decision-making; Iterative refinement and workflow optimization. Strengths: Adaptable to real-time changes; Scalable for multi-domain tasks; High accuracy.

The header row is shaded grey. The Paradigm column is printed in bold. There are no footnotes, units or numeric values in this table; every cell is qualitative text.

LABEL: Figure 7
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 7: An Overview of AI Agents
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 7: An Overview of AI Agents. A hub-and-spoke diagram: one central agent node with three surrounding capability groups drawn as rounded panels.

Centre: a magenta box holding two small chips labelled "Task" and "Role" on its top row, and below them a node-graph icon marked "LLM" followed by the text "+ Agent". This is the agent itself — an LLM combined with a task and a role.

Upper-left group: a peach rounded panel titled "Memory" containing two boxes, "Short-term" and "Long-term". An elbow arrow leaves the central agent box, runs up and left, and terminates with an arrowhead at the Memory panel.

Lower-left group: a blue rounded panel titled "Planning" containing a box "Reflection", an ellipsis "...", and a box "Self-critics". An elbow arrow leaves the central agent box, runs down and left, and terminates with an arrowhead at the Planning panel.

Right group: a blue rounded panel titled "Tools" containing, top to bottom, a box "Vector Search X", a box "Web Search", an ellipsis "...", and a box "API". A thick arrow runs from the Tools panel left into the central agent box. Separately, a double-headed arrow connects the "Vector Search X" box to a green box labelled "Data Sources" at the far right, indicating a two-way link between the vector-search tool and the external data.

Read together, the figure asserts the four-part composition of an AI agent — an LLM with a defined task and role at the centre, memory split into short-term and long-term, planning that includes reflection and self-critique, and a tool belt (vector search, web search, APIs) that reaches external data sources. The ellipses in the Planning and Tools panels indicate the lists are non-exhaustive.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 3 Core Principles and Background of Agentic Intelligence > 3.2 Planning
LABEL: Figure 9
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 9: Overview of Agentic Planning and Tool Use
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 9: Overview of Agentic Planning and Tool Use. One image containing two side-by-side sub-panels with their own sub-captions: "(a) An Overview of Agentic Planning" on the left and "(b) An Overview of Tool Use" on the right. The body text refers to them as Figure 9a and 9b.

Panel (a), Agentic Planning. A blue box "User Input" has a right-pointing arrow into a node-graph "LLM" icon. From the LLM an upward arrow points to a peach box "Response". Below the LLM a double-headed vertical arrow connects it to a pink box "Planning", so planning and the LLM exchange information in both directions. From "Planning" a downward arrow goes to a green box "Task Decomposition"; from there a downward arrow goes to a grey box "Plan Selection". From "Plan Selection" a left-pointing arrow goes to a blue box "External Planner"; from "External Planner" an upward arrow goes to a yellow box "Reflection & Refinement"; from there an upward arrow goes to a pale-cyan box "Memory Augmented Planning"; and from "Memory Augmented Planning" a right-pointing arrow returns into "Planning". Panel (a) is therefore an explicit closed cycle: Planning -> Task Decomposition -> Plan Selection -> External Planner -> Reflection & Refinement -> Memory Augmented Planning -> back to Planning, with the LLM attached to Planning and emitting the Response.

Panel (b), Tool Use. A blue box "User Input" has a right-pointing arrow into a node-graph "LLM" icon. From the LLM an upward arrow points to a peach box "Response", and a right-pointing arrow goes to a pink box "Reasoning". From "Reasoning" a downward arrow goes to a green box "Tools"; a double-headed vertical arrow connects "Tools" with a grey box "Environment". From "Environment" a left-pointing arrow goes to a white rounded box "Revised Response", and from "Revised Response" an upward arrow returns into the LLM. Panel (b) is therefore also a closed cycle: LLM -> Reasoning -> Tools <-> Environment -> Revised Response -> back to the LLM.

Both panels share the same entry (User Input) and exit (Response) shape, and both make the agentic refinement explicit as a drawn return edge.

Figure 10: An Overview of MultiAgent. A small four-node diagram showing one externally-facing agent and two peer agents, arranged as a triangle beneath a linear query-to-response path.

The agents carry no role or specialisation labels, no tools are drawn, and no memory or planning component is shown; the figure asserts only the communication topology. The body text supplies the interpretation: subtasks are distributed among specialised agents that communicate and share intermediate results, each operating with its own memory and workflow.

text:
TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 4 Agentic Workflow Patterns: Adaptive Strategies for Dynamic Collaboration > 4.1 Prompt Chaining: Enhancing Accuracy Through Sequential Processing
LABEL: Figure 11
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 11: Illustration of Prompt Chaining Workflow
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 11: Illustration of Prompt Chaining Workflow. A single left-to-right sequential chain with one conditional gate that can terminate the chain early.

Path: a blue box labelled "Query" has a solid arrow into the first node-graph "LLM" icon. From that LLM a solid arrow runs right into a green diamond labelled "Gate". The diamond splits into two labelled branches drawn as an elbow fork on its right side:
  - the upper branch is labelled "Yes" and continues into a second "LLM" icon; from that second LLM a solid arrow runs into a third "LLM" icon; from the third LLM a solid arrow runs into a blue box labelled "Response".
  - the lower branch is labelled "Exit" and terminates there: no further node, box or arrow follows it.

There are therefore three LLM stages in total (one before the gate, two after it), exactly one decision point, and no loops or back edges. The gate is a pass/abort check on the first stage's output rather than a router between alternatives: only the "Yes" side proceeds, and "Exit" stops the workflow.

This matches the definition in the body text of prompt chaining as a decomposition of a complex task into fixed sequential steps where each step builds on the previous one, at the cost of added latency from the sequential processing.

- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 4.1 defines the prompt chaining pattern that the sequential LLM chain in the figure illustrates.
- Section 4.1 states the accuracy/latency trade-off of the sequential arrangement drawn in the figure.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 4 Agentic Workflow Patterns: Adaptive Strategies for Dynamic Collaboration > 4.2 Routing:Directing Inputs to Specialized Processes
LABEL: Figure 12
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 12: Illustration Routing Workflow
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 12: Illustration Routing Workflow. A one-in, three-way-branch, one-out diagram: a single query is classified by a router and sent down exactly one of three parallel specialised paths, all of which lead to the same response node.

Path: a blue box labelled "Query" has a solid arrow into a green diamond labelled "Router". Three branches leave the Router — one rising to the upper LLM, one running straight across to the middle LLM, and one descending to the lower LLM. Each branch ends with an arrowhead at a separate node-graph "LLM" icon, so three distinct LLM instances are drawn.

From each of the three LLM icons an edge runs right and converges on a single blue box labelled "Response": the upper LLM's edge turns down into the top of the Response box, the middle LLM's edge enters horizontally, and the lower LLM's edge turns up into the bottom of the Response box.

The branches carry no condition labels — the figure names neither the routing criterion nor the specialisation of each LLM. The body text supplies that interpretation: routing classifies an input and directs it to an appropriate specialised prompt or process, for example splitting customer-service queries into technical support, refund requests or general inquiries, or sending simple queries to smaller models and complex ones to advanced models.

Structurally this figure is the exclusive-choice counterpart of Figure 13 (Parallelization): there, all three LLMs run and an Aggregator merges them; here, the Router selects one path.

- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 4.2 defines the routing pattern drawn as the Router diamond with three specialised branches.
- Section 4.2 gives an example of the routing criterion; the criterion itself is not labelled in the figure.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 4 Agentic Workflow Patterns: Adaptive Strategies for Dynamic Collaboration > 4.3 Parallelization: Speeding Up Processing Through Concurrent Execution
LABEL: Figure 13
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 13: Illustration of Parallelization Workflow
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 13: Illustration of Parallelization Workflow. A fan-out/fan-in diagram: one input is dispatched simultaneously to three LLM workers whose outputs are merged by an aggregator.

Path: a blue box labelled "Query" on the left has three outgoing edges — one rising to an upper node-graph "LLM" icon, one running straight across to a middle "LLM" icon, and one descending to a lower "LLM" icon. All three arrows carry arrowheads into their respective LLM icons, so the three branches execute concurrently from the same input.

From each of the three LLM icons an edge runs right and converges on a green diamond labelled "Aggregator": the upper edge turns down into the top of the diamond, the middle edge enters horizontally, and the lower edge turns up into the bottom of the diamond.

From the "Aggregator" a single solid arrow runs right into a terminal blue box. That terminal box is labelled "Query" in the image — the same word as the input box — and not "Response" as in the neighbouring workflow figures.

There are no conditions, gates or loops in the figure. The two variants that the body text distinguishes — sectioning (independent subtasks) and voting (multiple outputs for accuracy) — are not labelled in the image; the three branches are drawn identically and without annotations, so the figure alone does not say which variant is depicted.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 4.3 defines parallelization and its two variants; the variants are not distinguished in the figure.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- Suspicious original label: the terminal node after the Aggregator is labelled "Query", duplicating the input label, whereas the parallel workflow figures 11, 12, 14 and 15 all terminate in a box labelled "Response". This looks like a labelling error in the original figure, but it is reported as printed and NOT corrected here.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 4 Agentic Workflow Patterns: Adaptive Strategies for Dynamic Collaboration > 4.4 Orchestrator-Workers: Dynamic Task Delegation
LABEL: Figure 14
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 14: Illustration of Orchestrator-Workers Workflow
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 14: Illustration of Orchestrator-Workers Workflow. A fan-out/fan-in diagram with a dedicated decomposition node at the front and a dedicated synthesis node at the back — the two diamonds are what distinguish it from the plain Parallelization figure.

Path: a blue box labelled "Query" has a solid arrow into a green diamond labelled "Orchestrator". Three branches leave the Orchestrator — one rising, one horizontal, one descending — each ending with an arrowhead at a separate node-graph "LLM" icon. These three LLM icons are the worker models.

From each of the three LLM icons an edge runs right and converges on a second green diamond labelled "Synthesizer": the upper edge turns down into the top of the diamond, the middle edge enters horizontally, and the lower edge turns up into the bottom. From the "Synthesizer" a single solid arrow runs right into a blue box labelled "Response".

There are no condition labels, no gates and no loops. The number of workers drawn (three) is illustrative; the body text stresses that, unlike parallelization, this workflow adapts to varying input complexity and the subtasks are not predefined — the orchestrator decides the decomposition dynamically. That dynamism is not itself rendered in the image; the image shows only the static orchestrator -> workers -> synthesizer topology.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 4.4 defines the orchestrator-workers pattern and contrasts it with parallelization.
- Section 4.4 states the applicability condition for this workflow.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 4 Agentic Workflow Patterns: Adaptive Strategies for Dynamic Collaboration > 4.5 Evaluator-Optimizer: Refining Output Through Iteration
LABEL: Figure 15
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 15: Illustration of Evaluator-Optimizer Workflow
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 15: Illustration of Evaluator-Optimizer Workflow. A two-model loop with a labelled accept edge and a labelled reject-with-feedback return edge — the only workflow figure in this section that draws an explicit refinement cycle.

Nodes: a blue box labelled "Query" on the left; a node-graph "LLM" icon captioned "Generator" beneath it; a second node-graph "LLM" icon captioned "Evaluator"; a blue box labelled "Response" on the right.

Edges and their labels:
  - "Query" -> "Generator" (solid arrow, unlabelled).
  - An arc above the two models runs from the "Generator" to the "Evaluator" and is labelled "Solution"; the arrowhead lands on the Evaluator.
  - "Evaluator" -> "Response" (solid arrow), labelled "Accepted" above the arrow.
  - An arc below the two models runs from the "Evaluator" back to the "Generator" and is labelled "Rejected+ Feedback" (printed with the plus sign attached to "Rejected"); the arrowhead lands on the Generator.

The loop is therefore explicit and conditional: the generator produces a candidate solution, the evaluator either accepts it — in which case it leaves as the response — or rejects it and returns feedback to the generator for another iteration. The two roles are drawn as two distinct LLM instances rather than as one model self-critiquing. No stopping criterion, iteration limit or evaluation rubric is shown in the image.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 4.5 defines the evaluator-optimizer pattern drawn as the Generator/Evaluator loop.
- Section 4.5 states the applicability condition; the criteria themselves are not drawn in the figure.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- The in-image label is printed as "Rejected+ Feedback" (no space before the plus sign); preserved verbatim.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 5 Taxonomy of Agentic RAG Systems > Workflow
LABEL: Figure 16
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 16: An Overview of Single Agentic RAG
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 16: An Overview of Single Agentic RAG. One routing agent mediates between the prompt and a set of retrieval tools, then hands context to an LLM for the answer.

Input path (top left, left to right): the word "Input" with a solid arrow into a blue box containing an envelope icon and the word "Query"; from "Query" a solid arrow into a peach box labelled "Prompt"; from "Prompt" a downward arrow into a pink diamond labelled "Retrieval Router Agent" (the label is set on three lines).

Tool access: a double-headed connection runs between the "Retrieval Router Agent" and a grey rounded panel titled "Tools". The Tools panel contains three boxes stacked top to bottom: "Vector Search X" (with a database-cylinder icon), "Vector Search Y" (with a database-cylinder icon), and "Web Search" (with a laptop/globe icon).

External data: a double-headed arrow connects "Vector Search X" to a light-green box labelled "Data Sources" (with a document icon), and a second double-headed arrow connects "Vector Search Y" to a darker-green box also labelled "Data Sources". "Web Search" has no drawn link to an external box.

Output path: from the left side of the "Retrieval Router Agent" a solid arrow points into a node-graph "LLM" icon, and from the LLM a solid arrow points left to the word "Response".

The figure's structural claim is centralisation: exactly one agent (the Retrieval Router Agent) performs the source selection, and all tool traffic passes through it before a single LLM synthesises the answer. The tool set drawn (two vector searches plus a web search) is narrower than the four knowledge-source types enumerated in the body text of Section 5.1.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 5.1 introduces Figure 16 as the single-agent, centralised routing architecture.
- Section 5.1 lists Text-to-SQL structured database access as one of the knowledge-source options; it is not drawn in the figure.
- Section 5.1 describes the dynamic routing behaviour of the single agent drawn as the Retrieval Router Agent.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- The tool set drawn in the figure (Vector Search X, Vector Search Y, Web Search) is a subset of the four knowledge-source categories enumerated in Section 5.1 (structured databases via Text-to-SQL, semantic search, web search, recommendation systems). The figure is described as drawn; the extra categories are attributed only to the text.

Figure 17: An Overview of Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Systems. The multi-agent counterpart of Figure 16: the single routing agent now delegates to three named retrieval agents, each of which owns a different slice of the tool belt.

Input path: the word "Input" with a solid arrow into a blue box containing an envelope icon and the word "Query"; a downward arrow from "Query" into a peach box labelled "Prompt"; a downward arrow from "Prompt" into a pink diamond labelled "Retrieval Router Agent".

Delegation: from the right side of the "Retrieval Router Agent" a double-headed connection fans out to three pale-yellow rounded boxes stacked vertically: "Retrieval Agent X" (top), "Retrieval Agent Y" (middle), "Retrieval Agent Z" (bottom).

Tools (inside a grey rounded "Tools" panel on the right), bound to specific agents:
  - "Retrieval Agent X" <-> "Vector Search X" and <-> "Vector Search Y" (both with database-cylinder icons).
  - "Retrieval Agent Y" <-> "Web Search" (laptop/globe icon).
  - "Retrieval Agent Z" <-> "MAIL" and <-> "CHAT".

External data: "Vector Search X" is joined by a double-headed arrow to a light-green box labelled "Data Sources"; "Vector Search Y" is joined by a double-headed arrow to a darker-green box labelled "Data Sources".

Output path: from the left side of the "Retrieval Router Agent" a solid arrow points into a node-graph "LLM" icon, and from the LLM a downward arrow points to the word "Response".

The figure therefore shows three specialised retrieval agents operating in parallel under one router, with results converging on a single LLM for synthesis. Note that the figure draws three agents (X, Y, Z) whereas the body text of Section 5.2 enumerates four (Agent 1 to Agent 4, including a recommendation-systems agent), and the figure's MAIL and CHAT tools are not among the tool types named in the text.

ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 17: An Overview of Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Systems. The multi-agent counterpart of Figure 16: the single routing agent now delegates to three named retrieval agents, each of which owns a different slice of the tool belt.

Input path: the word "Input" with a solid arrow into a blue box containing an envelope icon and the word "Query"; a downward arrow from "Query" into a peach box labelled "Prompt"; a downward arrow from "Prompt" into a pink diamond labelled "Retrieval Router Agent".

Delegation: from the right side of the "Retrieval Router Agent" a double-headed connection fans out to three pale-yellow rounded boxes stacked vertically: "Retrieval Agent X" (top), "Retrieval Agent Y" (middle), "Retrieval Agent Z" (bottom).

Tools (inside a grey rounded "Tools" panel on the right), bound to specific agents:
  - "Retrieval Agent X" <-> "Vector Search X" and <-> "Vector Search Y" (both with database-cylinder icons).
  - "Retrieval Agent Y" <-> "Web Search" (laptop/globe icon).
  - "Retrieval Agent Z" <-> "MAIL" and <-> "CHAT".

External data: "Vector Search X" is joined by a double-headed arrow to a light-green box labelled "Data Sources"; "Vector Search Y" is joined by a double-headed arrow to a darker-green box labelled "Data Sources".

Output path: from the left side of the "Retrieval Router Agent" a solid arrow points into a node-graph "LLM" icon, and from the LLM a downward arrow points to the word "Response".

The figure therefore shows three specialised retrieval agents operating in parallel under one router, with results converging on a single LLM for synthesis. Note that the figure draws three agents (X, Y, Z) whereas the body text of Section 5.2 enumerates four (Agent 1 to Agent 4, including a recommendation-systems agent), and the figure's MAIL and CHAT tools are not among the tool types named in the text.

ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 18: An illustration of Hierarchical Agentic RAG. A two-tier delegation tree drawn with five labelled boxes and four solid, single-headed arrows.

Top tier: a blue box labelled "Query" has a right-pointing arrow into a peach box labelled "Master Agent"; the "Master Agent" has a right-pointing arrow into a green box labelled "Response". So the master agent is the only node that touches the user-facing query and the final answer.

Lower tier: from the bottom of the "Master Agent" a single line drops and then splits into a horizontal bus that fans out to three downward arrows, each terminating with an arrowhead at one of three boxes: "Sub-Agent X" (pale cyan, left), "Sub-Agent Y" (yellow, centre), "Sub-Agent Z" (pink, right).

Direction: every arrow between the master and the sub-agents points downward only. No return arrow from any sub-agent back to the master agent is drawn, even though the workflow described in the body text has the higher-level agent collect and synthesise the subordinate agents' results before responding. The figure also draws only two tiers, whereas the worked example in the text names a top-tier agent, a mid-level agent and lower-level agent(s).

No tools, data sources, specialisations or condition labels are attached to any sub-agent; the figure asserts only the delegation topology.

- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 5.3 describes the hierarchy that the master/sub-agent tree in the figure depicts.
- Section 5.3 describes the upward aggregation step, which the figure does not draw as a return edge.
- The Section 5.3 worked example names a mid-level tier that the two-tier figure does not show.

- The figure draws only downward delegation arrows; the aggregation/return path described in Section 5.3 is not rendered. The figure also shows two tiers where the text's worked example describes three. Reported as drawn.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 5 Taxonomy of Agentic RAG Systems > 5.4 Agentic Corrective RAG
LABEL: Figure 19
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 19: Overview of Agentic Corrective RAG
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 19: Overview of Agentic Corrective RAG. A flowchart with one decision diamond and two labelled branches that rejoin at the LLM. All nodes are drawn in pink; process steps are ellipses, the decision is a diamond, and the query is a rectangle.

Entry chain (bottom left, running upward): a rectangle labelled "Query" has an upward arrow into an ellipse labelled "Context Retrieval"; "Context Retrieval" has an upward arrow into an ellipse labelled "Relevance Assessor"; "Relevance Assessor" has a right-pointing arrow into a diamond labelled "Is Document relevant".

Branches out of the diamond (verified on an enlarged crop of the image):
  - the UPPER branch is labelled "No" and runs as a long straight horizontal arrow directly to a node-graph "LLM" icon at the top right;
  - the LOWER branch is labelled "Yes" and leads to an ellipse labelled "Query Refinement", which has a right-pointing arrow into an ellipse labelled "Web Search (Tool)", from which an edge turns upward into the same "LLM" icon.

Exit: from the "LLM" icon a solid arrow points right to the word "Response".

There is no loop back to "Context Retrieval" or to the relevance check: the corrective path is a single forward detour through query refinement and web search before generation.

Naming: the figure's node names are "Context Retrieval", "Relevance Assessor", "Query Refinement" and "Web Search (Tool)", which correspond to but do not exactly match the five agents named in Section 5.4 (Context Retrieval Agent, Relevance Evaluation Agent, Query Refinement Agent, External Knowledge Retrieval Agent, Response Synthesis Agent). The Response Synthesis Agent has no named node in the figure; only a generic LLM icon appears in that position.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 5.4 states that documents judged NOT relevant are the ones that trigger the corrective path.
- Section 5.4 states that the web-search step is taken when the retrieved context is insufficient.
- Section 5.4 enumerates five agents; the figure names only four process nodes plus a generic LLM icon.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- Suspicious original labels / figure-versus-text conflict: in the image the "No" branch of "Is Document relevant" goes STRAIGHT to the LLM while the "Yes" branch goes through Query Refinement and Web Search. Section 5.4 says the opposite - documents below the relevance threshold (i.e. not relevant) are what trigger the corrective steps. The branch labels therefore appear to be swapped in the original figure. Verified on an enlarged crop; reported as printed and deliberately NOT corrected.
- Node names in the figure differ from the agent names in Section 5.4 ("Relevance Assessor" vs "Relevance Evaluation Agent"; no node corresponds to the "Response Synthesis Agent").

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 5 Taxonomy of Agentic RAG Systems > 5.5 Adaptive Agentic RAG
LABEL: Figure 20
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 20: An Overview of Adaptive Agentic RAG
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 20: An Overview of Adaptive Agentic RAG. A left-to-right flowchart with three decision diamonds and two explicit back edges. All nodes are pink; process steps are ellipses, decisions are diamonds, the query is a rectangle.

Entry chain (bottom left, running upward): a rectangle labelled "Query" -> an ellipse labelled "Retrieve (Node)" -> an ellipse labelled "Graph (Node)" -> a right-pointing arrow into the first diamond, labelled "Is Document relevant".

Decision 1, "Is Document relevant": two labelled stubs leave its right side, "No" (upper) and "Yes" (lower). Next along the row is an ellipse labelled "Generate (Node)".

Middle: "Generate (Node)" has a right-pointing arrow into the second diamond, labelled "Hallucin ation?" (the word is broken across two lines in the image). Two labelled stubs leave its right side: "No" (upper, printed as "N" over "o" on two lines) and "Yes" (lower). From the "Yes" side a line descends, turns left and re-enters the bottom of "Generate (Node)" with an arrowhead — i.e. a detected hallucination sends the flow back to regenerate.

Right: the third diamond is labelled "Answer Questions". Two labelled stubs leave its right side: "Yes" (upper), which carries a solid arrow to the word "Answer", and "No" (lower), from which a long line descends, runs all the way left across the figure and re-enters "Retrieve (Node)" with an arrowhead — i.e. an answer that does not address the question sends the flow back to retrieval.

Two loops are therefore drawn: a short regeneration loop (Hallucination? = Yes -> Generate) and a long re-retrieval loop (Answer Questions? = No -> Retrieve). The figure does not depict the query-complexity classifier or the three-way straightforward/simple/complex strategy selection that Section 5.5 describes as the core of Adaptive RAG.

SOURCE CONTEXT (identity statements bound to the original source file):
- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image.
- Section 5.5 describes the classifier-driven strategy selection that Figure 20 is said to illustrate.
- Section 5.5 enumerates the classifier, dynamic strategy selection and LLM integration components.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- Incomplete edges in the original figure: the "No"/"Yes" stubs of the "Is Document relevant" diamond and the "No" stub of the "Hallucin ation?" diamond are drawn without connecting arrows into the next node. Verified on 2x crops. Reported rather than inferred away.
- Figure-versus-text divergence: the figure shows a relevance/hallucination/answer-check loop, but does not show the query-complexity classifier or the straightforward/simple/complex three-way strategy selection that Section 5.5 presents as the defining mechanism of Adaptive RAG.
- The node label "Hallucin ation?" is broken across two lines in the image and is transcribed as printed.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 5 Taxonomy of Agentic RAG Systems > 5.6.1 Agent-G: Agentic Framework for Graph RAG
LABEL: Figure 21
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 21: An Overview of Agent-G: Agentic Framework for Graph RAG [8]
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 21: An Overview of Agent-G: Agentic Framework for Graph RAG [8]. A four-group architecture diagram (Retriever Bank, Agent, Generator, Critic Module) with an accept/reject feedback loop; the caption carries the citation [8] to the Agent-G paper.

Inputs: a database icon labelled "Database" at the top left has a downward arrow into the green panel titled "Retriever Bank", and also an elbow line running right toward the "Agent" box. A speech-bubble-with-question-mark icon labelled "Question" at the top centre has a downward arrow into a blue box labelled "Agent" (drawn with a robot icon).

Retriever Bank (green panel, left): the incoming edge passes through a small unlabelled diamond that splits into two parallel columns. The left column is a chain of three icon-labelled stages: "Graph" (node-and-edge icon) -> "Retriever" (database-with-magnifier icon) -> "Ranker" (star-over-podium icon). The right column is the same chain for text: "Text" (document-stack icon) -> "Retriever" -> "Ranker". So the bank holds one graph retrieval pipeline and one text retrieval pipeline, each with its own retriever and ranker.

Generation: the outputs of both Rankers run down and along the bottom into a yellow box labelled "Generator" (gear icons).

Critic Module (purple panel, right): the Generator's output runs right and up into this panel. The panel contains a "Validator" (gavel icon) at the bottom, an unlabelled decision diamond above it, and a "Commentor" (exclamation-mark speech box) to its left. LABEL: Figure 22
OBJECT IDENTITY: Figure 22: An Overview of GeAR: Graph-Enhanced Agent for Retrieval-Augmented Generation[37]
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Figure 22: An Overview of GeAR: Graph-Enhanced Agent for Retrieval-Augmented Generation[37]. A dense two-region system diagram reproduced from the GeAR paper cited as [37], with a legend box at the bottom. Solid edges denote the single-step process and dotted edges denote the multi-step process.

Region 1 (blue, upper/left), titled "Retrieval w/ SyncGE":
  - "original query q" enters from the left into a box "Base Retriever". A dotted edge labelled "updated query q^(n)" arrives at the Base Retriever from the far right, closing the multi-step loop.
  - "Base Retriever" emits "passages C'_q" rightward into a box "Reader", and also emits "passages C'_q" downward on the left and "triples T_q" downward in the middle.
  - "Reader" emits "proximal triples T'_q" leftward into a small node labelled "tripleLink".
  - An inner box titled "Graph Expansion" contains "Diverse Triple Beam Search", which emits "passages C~_q".
  - "passages C'_q" and "passages C~_q" converge on a Y-shaped merge node labelled "RRF" (reciprocal rank fusion).
  - From that RRF node an arrow runs left to the labelled "single-step output C_q".

Region 2 (orange, lower/right), titled "Multi-step Extension":
  - "passages C_q" feeds a box "Gist Memory Constructor".
  - The Gist Memory Constructor writes dotted edges labelled "proximal triples T^G_q(n)" into a cylinder labelled "Gist Memory G^(n)".
  - "Gist Memory" feeds a diamond labelled "stop?". The "N" branch leads to a box "Rewriter"; the Rewriter emits the dotted "updated query q^(n)" that returns to the Base Retriever. The "Y" branch, annotated G^(n), leads toward a node labelled "passageLink".
  - Passages "C_t1, ..., C_t|G(n)|" feed a second Y-shaped merge node labelled "RRF", which produces the labelled "multi-step output C^(n)_q".

Legend box (bottom): eight entries - "original query" (grey striped down-arrow), "updated query" (grey down-arrow), "single-step process" (solid down-arrow), "multi-step process" (dotted down-arrow), "triples index" (blue down-arrow), "passages index" (magenta striped down-arrow), "accumulate iteratively" (fine dotted down-arrow), "LLM-based component" (thick rounded rectangle outline). Boxes drawn with the thick rounded outline - Reader, Gist Memory Constructor, Rewriter - are therefore marked as LLM-based components.

The figure's structural claim: a base retriever plus graph expansion via diverse triple beam search, fused by RRF, gives the single-step output; an agentic multi-step extension adds a gist memory, a stop decision and a query rewriter that loops updated queries back into the base retriever, giving the multi-step output.

- The printed caption in the source Markdown matches the caption rendered in the image, including the [37] citation.
- Section 5.6.2 defines the graph expansion mechanism drawn as the "Graph Expansion" inner box of the figure.

- Section 5.6.2 states the multi-hop purpose of the graph expansion module.

KNOWN ISSUES AND UNREADABLE PARTS:
- The mathematical notation uses small subscripts and superscripts. The symbols transcribed above (C'_q, C~_q, T_q, T'_q, T^G_q(n), G^(n), C_t1 ... C_t|G(n)|, q^(n), C^(n)_q) are rendered here in plain ASCII; the tilde on C~_q is an overset tilde and the script G is a calligraphic G in the original.
- The precise routing of a few dotted edges in the crowded centre-right of the figure (between Gist Memory, stop?, passageLink and the second RRF node) is hard to trace at the available resolution; the component names and branch labels are legible, but the edge-by-edge topology in that sub-region is reported only to the extent it is clearly legible.
- BM25 is named as an example base retriever in the body text but does not appear as a label inside the figure.

Figure 23: An Overview of Agentic Document Workflows (ADW) [38]. A hand-drawn-style, left-to-right architecture sketch with four groups; the image carries its own internal title "Agentic Document Workflows" (with a robot emoji and a document emoji) at the top left.

Left group - "Input Document": a card showing a sample invoice. The legible parts of the sample are the vendor line "ACME Office Supply, Inc." at the top left and the word "INVOICE" at the top right, plus faint column headings for quantity/description/unit price/total and a totals block. The body text of the invoice is rendered too small to read reliably and is not transcribed here. An arrow points from this card into the centre group.

Centre group - "Agent Workflow" (pink rounded container): three rounded boxes. Two sit side by side on the upper row: "Parse + Extract Structured Data" (left) and "Apply Rules Generate Actions" (right). One sits centred below them: "Maintain State Track Context".

Right group - "Structured Recommendations" (card with a lightbulb icon): a bulleted list of four output types: "Case Summary", "Compliance Report", "Claim Decision", "Payments Plan". An arrow points from the Agent Workflow container into this card.

Bottom group - "Knowledge Base": a card showing a thumbnail of a reference document with a blue/green logo; the logo text appears to read "NATIONAL GENERAL" but the rest of that thumbnail is illegible at this resolution. Two curved arrows connect this card with the Agent Workflow container, one running down from the workflow to the knowledge base and one running back up, i.e. a bidirectional retrieval/feedback link.

Overall direction: Input Document -> Agent Workflow -> Structured Recommendations, with the Agent Workflow exchanging information with the Knowledge Base. The three inner boxes correspond to the parsing, rule-application and state-maintenance steps of the ADW workflow described in Section 5.7.

TITLE: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
SECTION: 6 Comparative Analysis of Agentic RAG Frameworks
LABEL: Table 2
OBJECT IDENTITY: Table 2: Comparative Analysis: Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG vs Agentic Document Workflows (ADW)
ENRICHED VISUAL RECORD:
ENRICHED DESCRIPTION (author-verified against the original image):
Table 2: Comparative Analysis: Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG vs Agentic Document Workflows (ADW), from the survey "Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG" (Singh et al.), page 29, Section 6. The title is printed above the table in the image. Four columns - "Feature", "Traditional RAG", "Agentic RAG", "Agentic Document Workflows (ADW)" - and ten feature rows. All cells are qualitative text; there are no numbers, units or footnotes. Full contents, row by row:

Focus | Isolated retrieval and generation tasks | Multi-agent collaboration and reasoning | Document-centric end-to-end workflows
Context Maintenance | Limited | Enabled through memory modules | Maintains state across multi-step workflows
Dynamic Adaptability | Minimal | High | Tailored to document workflows
Workflow Orchestration | Absent | Orchestrates multi-agent tasks | Integrates multi-step document processing
Use of External Tools/APIs | Basic integration (e.g., retrieval tools) | Extends via tools like APIs and knowledge bases | Deeply integrates business rules and domain-specific tools
Scalability | Limited to small datasets or queries | Scalable for multi-agent systems | Scales for multi-domain enterprise workflows
Complex Reasoning | Basic (e.g., simple Q&A) | Multi-step reasoning with agents | Structured reasoning across documents
Primary Applications | QA systems, knowledge retrieval | Multi-domain knowledge and reasoning | Contract review, invoice processing, claims analysis
Strengths | Simplicity, quick setup | High accuracy, collaborative reasoning | End-to-end automation, domain-specific intelligence

Table 3: Taxonomy-Driven Comparison of Agentic RAG Architectures, from the survey "Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG" (Singh et al.), page 33, Section 10.2. Agent Cardinality | Single | Multiple | Multiple (tiered) | Multiple
Control Structure | Centralized | Flat | Hierarchical / evaluator-based | Adaptive / structured
Knowledge Representation | Unstructured | Unstructured or hybrid | Unstructured or hybrid | Graph-based or document-centric
Knowledge Dependency | Low | Moderate | Moderate | High, sensitive to graph quality
Reasoning Mode | Implicit, LLM-driven | Distributed across agents | Strategic with supervisory control | Relational or symbolic + LLM
Reasoning Depth | Low to moderate | Moderate to high | High | High, multi-hop reasoning
Retrieval Adaptivity | Limited | High | High | High
Scalability | Moderate | High | Moderate | Moderate
Latency | Low | Moderate | High | Moderate to high
Engineering Complexity | Low | Moderate | High | High
Best-Fit Scenarios | Simple QA and routing | Multi-domain synthesis | High-stakes, reliability-critical tasks | Knowledge-intensive, relational domains

The header row is shaded grey and the Dimension column is printed in bold. The four taxonomy dimensions that the survey's abstract names - agent cardinality, control structure, autonomy and knowledge representation - appear here as the first rows of the table, with Retrieval Adaptivity standing in for autonomy.
